notes.summary:
Computer security gives 2 to 3 questions in Tier 2. Most of them describe a threat and ask for its name (virus, worm, trojan, ransomware, phishing, DoS), or ask what a protection tool does (firewall, antivirus, encryption, digital signature).

Learn the one clue that tells each threat apart, which key is used for what, and the basics of the IT Act, 2000.

concepts.title: Security goals
concepts.body:
Computer security protects data and systems from harm and misuse. Its three goals are called the CIA triad:

GoalMeaningProtected by
ConfidentialityOnly the right people can read the dataEncryption, passwords
IntegrityData is not changed without permissionHashing, digital signatures
AvailabilityThe system works when users need itBackups, protection from DoS attacks
  • Authentication checks who you are (password, OTP, fingerprint). Authorisation decides what you are allowed to do.
  • Non-repudiation: the sender cannot later deny sending a message (given by a digital signature).

concepts.title: Malware
concepts.body:
Malware (malicious software) is any program written to harm a computer or steal from its user.

TypeHow to recognise it
VirusAttaches itself to a host file or program and spreads when that file is run or shared
WormCopies itself and spreads across a network on its own, with no host file and no user action
Trojan horseLooks like a useful or legitimate program but secretly does harm; does not copy itself
RansomwareLocks or encrypts your files and demands payment (ransom), often in Bitcoin. Example: WannaCry (2017)
SpywareSecretly watches what you do and sends your data to someone else
KeyloggerRecords every key you press to steal passwords. It can be software or a small hardware device
AdwareShows unwanted advertisements
RootkitHides deep in the system and gives an attacker administrator (root) control
BotnetA network of infected computers (bots or zombies) controlled by one attacker
Logic bomb / time bombStays quiet until a condition or a date is reached, then acts
BackdoorA hidden way into a system that skips the normal login
ScarewareShows fake alarms ("your PC is infected") to make you buy useless software

concepts.title: Types of viruses
concepts.body:
Virus typeWhat it does
Boot sector virusInfects the boot sector of a disk and runs when the computer starts
Macro virusWritten as a macro inside Word or Excel files
File infectorAttaches to program files such as .exe
Resident virusHides in the computer's memory (RAM), so it can act again even if the original file is deleted
Polymorphic virusChanges its code each time it spreads to avoid antivirus detection
Multipartite virusSpreads in more than one way (boot sector and files)
Stealth virusHides the changes it makes so antivirus cannot see it
  • Brain (1986, from Pakistan) is known as the first virus for IBM PCs.
  • Creeper (1971) is often called the first self-copying program.
  • Common signs of infection: the computer slows down, files go missing, strange pop-ups appear.

concepts.title: Phishing and social engineering
concepts.body:
Social engineering tricks people, not machines, into giving away secrets.

AttackChannel or trick
PhishingFake emails or websites that look like a bank or company, to steal passwords or card details
Spear phishingPhishing aimed at one particular person or group
WhalingPhishing aimed at top officials ("big fish")
VishingVoice phishing over phone calls
SmishingPhishing by SMS text message
PharmingRedirects you to a fake website even when you type the correct address (by changing DNS)
SpoofingFaking an email address, caller ID, IP address or website to look trusted
BaitingLeaving an infected pen drive or free offer for someone to pick up
Shoulder surfingWatching over someone's shoulder as they type a PIN
Identity theftUsing someone else's personal details to commit fraud

Spam is unwanted bulk email. It is not always an attack, but phishing often comes as spam.

concepts.title: Hacking and network attacks
concepts.body:
AttackWhat happens
DoS (denial of service)Floods a server with traffic so real users cannot reach it
DDoS (distributed DoS)The same, but from many computers at once, usually a botnet
Man-in-the-middleThe attacker secretly sits between two parties and reads or changes their messages
Sniffing / eavesdroppingCapturing data as it moves on a network
Brute-force attackTrying every possible password until one works
Dictionary attackTrying common words as passwords
SQL injectionTyping database commands into a website form to read or change its database
Cross-site scripting (XSS)Putting harmful script into a web page that other users then run
Zero-day attackUses a flaw the maker does not yet know about, so no fix exists
Session hijackingStealing a logged-in session (often through its cookie)
CryptojackingSecretly using your computer to mine cryptocurrency
  • Cookies are small files a website stores in your browser. Third-party (tracking) cookies follow you across sites and can expose your privacy.
  • Hacking is getting into a system without permission. Cracking usually means breaking software protection or passwords for harm.

concepts.title: Protection tools
concepts.body:
ToolWhat it does
FirewallFilters incoming and outgoing network traffic using set rules; can be hardware or software. It stands between a trusted network and the internet
AntivirusScans for, blocks and removes malware (Quick Heal, Norton, McAfee, Kaspersky, Windows Defender)
VPN (virtual private network)Creates an encrypted tunnel over the internet for private browsing
Two-factor / multi-factor authenticationAsks for two or more proofs: something you know (password), have (phone OTP) or are (fingerprint)
CAPTCHACompletely Automated Public Turing test to tell Computers and Humans Apart; stops bots
BiometricsIdentifies a person by fingerprint, face, iris or voice
Patches and automatic updatesFix security flaws; automatic updates install them without user action
BackupKeeps a copy of data so it can be restored after ransomware or a crash
IDS / IPSIntrusion detection / prevention system: watches traffic for attacks
HoneypotA fake system set up to attract and study attackers
SandboxA closed space where a doubtful program runs without touching the real system

Strong password: at least 8 to 12 characters, with capital and small letters, numbers and symbols; never your name or birth date; a different one for each site.

concepts.title: Encryption and keys
concepts.body:
• Plaintext: readable data. Ciphertext: scrambled, unreadable data.
  • Encryption turns plaintext into ciphertext; decryption turns it back. Both use a key. The study of this is cryptography.
Symmetric (secret key)Asymmetric (public key)
KeysOne shared key for both encrypting and decryptingA pair: a public key (shared with all) and a private key (kept secret)
SpeedFastSlower
ExamplesAES, DESRSA
  • To send a secret message: encrypt with the receiver's public key; only the receiver's private key can open it.
  • A hash function (such as SHA-256) turns data into a fixed-length value. It is one-way and is used to check integrity and store passwords.

concepts.title: Digital signatures, certificates and HTTPS
concepts.body:
• A digital signature is made with the sender's private key and checked with the sender's public key. It proves who sent the message (authentication), that it was not changed (integrity) and that the sender cannot deny it (non-repudiation).
  • A digital certificate links a public key to its owner. It is issued by a Certifying Authority (CA). In India, CAs are licensed by the Controller of Certifying Authorities (CCA) under the IT Act.
  • SSL/TLS encrypts data between your browser and a website. HTTPS is HTTP over TLS; it uses port 443 and the browser shows a padlock.
TaskKey used
Encrypt a secret message to BB's public key
Decrypt itB's private key
Sign a message as AA's private key
Verify A's signatureA's public key

concepts.title: Cyber law and hackers
concepts.body:
• Information Technology Act, 2000 is India's main cyber law. It came into force on 17 October 2000 and was amended in 2008. It gives legal status to electronic records and digital signatures.
  • Key sections: 43 damage to a computer system (compensation), 66 computer-related offences (hacking), 66C identity theft, 66D cheating by impersonation using a computer, 66E violation of privacy, 66F cyber terrorism, 67 publishing obscene material online.
  • Section 66A (offensive messages) was struck down by the Supreme Court in 2015 (Shreya Singhal case).
  • CERT-In (Indian Computer Emergency Response Team), under the Ministry of Electronics and IT, is the national agency for handling cyber security incidents.
  • Report cyber fraud on helpline 1930 or at cybercrime.gov.in.
  • The Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023 governs how personal data is handled.
Hacker typeWho they are
White hatEthical hacker who tests systems with permission
Black hatCriminal hacker who breaks in for gain or harm
Grey hatBreaks in without permission but without bad intent
Script kiddieUnskilled person using ready-made tools
HacktivistHacks to push a political or social cause

varieties.name: Malware and virus types
varieties.how: Look for the key clue: needs a host file (virus), spreads alone (worm), pretends to be useful (trojan), asks for money (ransomware), records keys (keylogger).

example.q: A program spreads from computer to computer over a network by itself, without attaching to any file. It is a:
steps: A virus needs a host file, so it is not a virus.
A trojan does not copy itself.
Spreading alone over a network is the mark of a worm.

varieties.name: Phishing and social engineering
varieties.how: Find the channel: email or fake site (phishing), phone call (vishing), SMS (smishing), correct address but fake site (pharming).

example.q: A caller pretends to be from your bank and asks for your OTP. This is called:
steps: Email tricks are phishing; SMS tricks are smishing.
A voice call trick is voice phishing.

varieties.name: Hacking and network attacks
varieties.how: Match the action: flooding (DoS, DDoS if many machines), sitting between two parties (man-in-the-middle), trying all passwords (brute force), code in a form (SQL injection).

example.q: Thousands of infected computers send requests to a website at the same time so that it crashes. What is this attack?
steps: Flooding a server so real users cannot reach it is denial of service.
Because many computers (a botnet) do it together, it is distributed.

varieties.name: Firewalls, antivirus and safe practices
varieties.how: Firewall filters traffic; antivirus removes malware; VPN hides traffic in an encrypted tunnel; 2FA adds a second proof; CAPTCHA stops bots.

example.q: Which security tool filters incoming and outgoing network traffic according to set rules?
steps: Antivirus scans files on the computer for malware.
A firewall checks network traffic against rules and blocks what is not allowed.

varieties.name: Encryption, keys and digital signatures
varieties.how: Secret message: receiver's public key to lock, receiver's private key to open. Signature: sender's private key to sign, sender's public key to check.

example.q: A sends a message to B that only B must be able to read. Which key does A use to encrypt it?
steps: Anyone can get B's public key, but only B has B's private key.
Locking with B's public key means only B's private key can unlock it.

varieties.name: Cyber law, agencies and hacker types
varieties.how: Remember IT Act 2000 (amended 2008), 66C identity theft, 66D cheating by impersonation, 66F cyber terrorism, CERT-In for incidents, 1930 helpline.

example.q: Under which section of the IT Act, 2000 is identity theft (using someone's password or digital signature) punished?
steps: Section 66 covers computer-related offences in general.
66C is identity theft; 66D is cheating by impersonation.

tips: Virus needs a host file; worm spreads by itself; trojan pretends to be useful.
Ransomware asks for money; spyware steals information; adware shows ads.
Phishing is by email, vishing by voice call, smishing by SMS.
A digital signature uses the sender's private key; encryption for secrecy uses the receiver's public key.
A firewall filters network traffic; it does not remove viruses from files.
HTTPS uses SSL/TLS and port 443; look for the padlock.
traps: A trojan does not copy itself; if the question says it spreads on its own, the answer is worm.
DoS comes from one source; DDoS comes from many (a botnet).
A keylogger can be hardware as well as software.
Do not sign with the public key: signing always uses the private key.
Pharming sends you to a fake site even when you type the right address; phishing needs you to click a fake link.

questions.q: Malware that copies itself and spreads across a network on its own, without attaching to a host file, is a:
questions.solution: A worm is self-replicating and travels across networks by itself. A virus needs a host file to spread.

questions.q: The main job of a firewall is to:
options: Filter incoming and outgoing network traffic
questions.solution: A firewall checks network traffic against rules and blocks what is not allowed. Removing viruses is the job of antivirus software.

questions.q: Sending fake emails that look like they come from a bank, to steal passwords, is called:
questions.solution: Phishing uses fake messages or websites to trick people into revealing passwords or card details.

questions.q: A program that pretends to be a useful game but secretly harms the computer is a:
questions.solution: A Trojan horse hides harmful code inside software that looks useful, like the wooden horse of Troy.

questions.q: Converting readable data (plaintext) into an unreadable form (ciphertext) is called:
questions.solution: Encryption converts plaintext to ciphertext so only someone with the key can read it. Decryption is the reverse.

questions.q: An attack that floods a website with so much traffic that real users cannot reach it is a:
questions.solution: A DoS attack overloads a server. When many computers (a botnet) do it together, it is a DDoS attack.

questions.q: WannaCry (2017), which locked files on computers worldwide and demanded Bitcoin payment, is an example of:
questions.solution: WannaCry encrypted victims' files and demanded a ransom in Bitcoin, which is exactly what ransomware does.

questions.q: A digital signature is created using the:
questions.solution: The sender signs with their own private key. Anyone can then verify the signature with the sender's public key, which proves who sent it and that it was not changed.

flashcards.back: Virus needs a host file; worm spreads on its own over networks
Malware disguised as useful software; does not self-replicate
Fake email or website / voice call / SMS
Distributed Denial of Service: many machines flood a server
Signed with sender's private key, verified with sender's public key
